facts.statement: The only recognized species of Elasmosaurus is Elasmosaurus platyurus.
facts.quote: species: platyurus

facts.statement: The genus Elasmosaurus was named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1868.
facts.quote: authority: Cope, 1868

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus fossils date to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Campanian)

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus lived in North America between 80.6 and 77 million years ago.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus () is a genus of plesiosaur that lived in North America during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, at about 80.6 to 77 million years ago.

facts.statement: The first Elasmosaurus specimen was discovered in 1867 near Fort Wallace, Kansas.
facts.quote: The first specimen was discovered in 1867 near Fort Wallace, Kansas, US

facts.statement: Only one incomplete Elasmosaurus skeleton is definitively known to science.
facts.quote: Only one incomplete Elasmosaurus skeleton is definitely known

facts.statement: The neck of Elasmosaurus was approximately 7.1 meters long.
facts.quote: The neck alone was around 7.1 m long.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus had 72 neck vertebrae, the second-highest number known for any animal, making it one of the longest-necked creatures to have lived.
facts.quote: Along with its relative Albertonectes, it was one of the longest-necked animals to have lived, with the second largest number of neck vertebrae known, 72, at least 3 fewer than Albertonectes.

facts.statement: The function of Elasmosaurus's long neck is unknown, though it may have been used for feeding.
facts.quote: It is unknown what their long necks were used for, but they may have had a function in feeding.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurids likely ate small fish and marine invertebrates, possibly using gastroliths to aid digestion.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurids probably ate small fish and marine invertebrates, seizing them with their long teeth, and may have used gastroliths (stomach stones) to help digest their food.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus fossils are found in the Pierre Shale formation, representing marine deposits from the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus is known from the Pierre Shale formation, which represents marine deposits from the Western Interior Seaway.

facts.statement: The first Elasmosaurus specimen was discovered in early 1867 by army surgeon Theophilus Hunt Turner and scout William Comstock near Fort Wallace, Kansas.
facts.quote: In early 1867, the American army surgeon Theophilus Hunt Turner and the army scout William "Medecine Bill" Comstock explored the rocks around Fort Wallace, Kansas

facts.statement: In December 1867, Turner and others recovered much of the vertebral column and other bones from the site, with the material weighing a combined 800 lbs.
facts.quote: In December 1867 Turner and others from Fort Wallace returned to the site and recovered much of the vertebral column, as well as concretions that contained other bones; the material had a combined weight of 800 lbs.

facts.statement: The specimen arrived in Philadelphia in March 1868, and Cope named it Elasmosaurus platyurus at the March ANSP meeting.
facts.quote: The specimen arrived in Philadelphia by rail in March 1868, whereafter Cope examined it hurriedly; he reported on it at the March ANSP meeting, during which he named it Elasmosaurus platyurus.

facts.statement: The generic name Elasmosaurus combines Greek words for 'metal plate' and 'lizard', referring to the plate-like bones in the sternal and pelvic regions.
facts.quote: The generic name Elasmosaurus is a portmanteau of the Ancient Greek ἔλᾰσμᾰ (élăsmă, "metal plate") prefixed onto σαῦρος (saûros, "lizard"), in reference to the "plate" bones of the sternal and pelvic regions.

facts.statement: The specific name platyurus means 'flat-tailed', referring to the compressed neck vertebrae and their laminae.
facts.quote: The specific name also comes from the Ancient Greek πλατύς (platýs, "flat") and ουρά (ourá, "tail"), all meaning "flat-tailed", in reference to the compressed "tail" (actually the neck) and laminae of the vertebrae there.

facts.statement: The discoverer, Theophilus Hunt Turner, died unexpectedly on July 27, 1869, before seeing the completion of the work on the specimen.
facts.quote: Turner died unexpectedly at Fort Wallace on July 27, 1869, without seeing the completion of the work he began

facts.statement: The circumstances of Turner's discovery remained unknown until his letters were published in 1987.
facts.quote: The circumstances around Turner's discovery of the type specimen were not covered in Cope's report, and remained unknown until Turner's letters were published in 1987.

facts.statement: Cope scientifically described and illustrated Elasmosaurus in 1869, based on a reconstruction he presented in September 1868.
facts.quote: In 1869 Cope scientifically described and figured Elasmosaurus, and the preprint version of the manuscript contained a reconstruction of the skeleton which he had earlier presented during his report at an ANSP meeting in September 1868.

facts.statement: Cope's initial reconstruction showed Elasmosaurus with a short neck, a long tail, and uncertain hind limbs.
facts.quote: The reconstruction showed Elasmosaurus with a short neck and a long tail, unlike other plesiosaurs, and Cope was also unsure whether it had hind limbs.

facts.statement: Cope mistakenly identified tail vertebrae as neck vertebrae because the jaws were found at that end of the skeleton.
facts.quote: Cope had apparently concluded that the tail vertebrae belonged to the neck, since the jaws had been found at that end of the skeleton, even though the opposite end terminated in the axis and atlas bones that are found in the neck.

facts.statement: Despite Cope's attempts to destroy the preprints, one copy reached Othniel Charles Marsh, who publicly mocked the error.
facts.quote: Though Cope had tried to destroy the preprints, one copy came to the attention of the American paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh, who made light of the mistake.

facts.statement: The mistake led to long-standing antagonism between Cope and Marsh, who repeatedly brought up the error for decades.
facts.quote: This led to antagonism between Cope, who was embarrassed by the mistake, and Marsh, who brought up the mistake repeatedly for decades.

facts.statement: The dispute gained widespread public attention in the 1890s when Marsh revisited the issue in the New York Herald.
facts.quote: Marsh returned to the issue during their controversy in the New York Herald in the 1890s (Marsh claimed he had pointed out the error to Cope immediately), when their dispute gained widespread public attention.

facts.statement: The argument over the reconstruction was part of the famous 'Bone Wars' rivalry and is well known in paleontological history.
facts.quote: The argument was part of the "Bone Wars" rivalry between the two, and is well known in the history of paleontology.

facts.statement: The function of Elasmosaurus's long neck is unknown, but it may have been used for feeding.
facts.quote: It is unknown what their long necks were used for, but they may have had a function in feeding.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope initially believed the original Elasmosaurus material represented two different animals, referring to one as Discosaurus carinatus in a 1868 letter.
facts.quote: Cope initially thought it consisted of two specimens of different animals – in an 1868 letter to LeConte, Cope had referred to the supposed "smaller specimen" as Discosaurus carinatus.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Elasmosaurus was not redescribed in detail until 2005 by German paleontologist Sven Sachs.
facts.quote: It was only redescribed in detail in 2005 by the German paleontologist Sven Sachs.

facts.statement: The only confirmed specimen of Elasmosaurus is the incomplete holotype cataloged as ANSP 10081.
facts.quote: Today, the incomplete holotype specimen, cataloged as ANSP 10081, is the only definite specimen of Elasmosaurus.

facts.statement: A missing neck vertebra was rediscovered in 2013, revising the count from 71 to 72 vertebrae.
facts.quote: In 2013 an incomplete neck vertebra centrum of the holotype that had been mentioned by Cope but thought to have been lost was rediscovered in storage by Sachs, and the neck vertebra count was revised from 71 to 72.

facts.statement: Fossils possibly belonging to the holotype were discovered by Benjamin Franklin Mudge in 1871 but are likely lost.
facts.quote: Fossils that may have belonged to the holotype were found by the American geologist Benjamin Franklin Mudge in 1871, but have probably been lost since.

facts.statement: Additional plesiosaur fossils, including vertebrae, ribs, and gastroliths, were found near the original site in 1954, 1991, 1994, and 1998.
facts.quote: Additional plesiosaur fossils were recovered near the original locality in 1954, 1991, 1994, and 1998, including back vertebrae, ribs, gastralia (belly ribs), and gastroliths.

facts.statement: In 2007, paleontologists Leslie Noè and Marcela Gómez-Pérez doubted that additional fossils found near the original site belonged to the type specimen or to Elasmosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2007 the Colombian paleontologists Leslie Noè and Marcela Gómez-Pérez expressed doubt that the additional elements belonged to the type specimen, or even to Elasmosaurus, due to lack of evidence.

facts.statement: In 2017, researchers suggested a fragmentary elasmosaurid skeleton from Germany may belong to Elasmosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2017 Sachs and Joachim Ladwig suggested that a fragmentary elasmosaurid skeleton from the upper Campanian of Kronsmoor in Schleswig-Holstein, Germany, and housed in the Naturkunde-Museum Bielefeld, may have belonged to Elasmosaurus.

facts.statement: A replica of the Elasmosaurus skeleton at the Fort Wallace Museum measures approximately 12.8 meters in length.
facts.quote: The replica at the Fort Wallace Museum measures about 12.8 m in length.

facts.statement: A polished stone found in a tail vertebra of the holotype is hypothesized to be a gastrolith.
facts.quote: He also noted that a small stone wedged in the neural canal of one of the tail vertebrae of the holotype may be a gastrolith, based on its polished appearance.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus had a neck estimated to be 7.1 meters long.
facts.quote: The neck of Elasmosaurus is estimated at 7.1 m in length

facts.statement: Related elasmosaurids indicate Elasmosaurus had a compact, streamlined body with long paddle-like limbs, a short tail, a small head, and an extremely long neck.
facts.quote: related elasmosaurids show it would have had a compact, streamlined body, long, paddle-like limbs, a short tail, a proportionately small head, and an extremely long neck

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus had a slender, triangular skull like other elasmosaurids.
facts.quote: Like other elasmosaurids, Elasmosaurus would have had a slender, triangular skull

facts.statement: The snout of Elasmosaurus was rounded and formed almost a semi-circle when viewed from above.
facts.quote: The snout was rounded and almost formed a semi-circle when viewed from above

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus likely had six large fang-like teeth in each premaxilla.
facts.quote: It probably had six teeth in each premaxilla, and the teeth preserved there were formed like large fangs

facts.statement: The teeth of Elasmosaurus interlocked and had slender, rounded crowns in cross-section.
facts.quote: The teeth interlocked, and their tooth crowns were slender and rounded in cross-section

facts.statement: The shoulder blades of Elasmosaurus were fused and met at the midline without a median bar.
facts.quote: The shoulder blades (scapulae) were fused and met at the midline, bearing no trace of a median bar

facts.statement: The pectoral paddles of Elasmosaurus were longer than the pelvic paddles.
facts.quote: The paddles at the front (the pectoral paddles) were longer than those at the back (the pelvic paddles)

facts.statement: In 1869, Cope estimated the length of Elasmosaurus at 13.1 meters by summing vertebral lengths and estimating missing parts.
facts.quote: Initially, in his 1869 description of Elasmosaurus, Cope estimated the length of the animal by summing up vertebral lengths and estimations of missing parts, resulting in a total length of 13.1 m

facts.statement: In 1952, Samuel Welles estimated the body length of Elasmosaurus to be 10.3 meters.
facts.quote: However, in 1952, the American paleontologist Samuel Welles estimated the body length to have been 10.3 m

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus had 72 neck vertebrae, a count higher than any other plesiosaur except Albertonectes.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus differed from all other plesiosaurs by having 72 neck vertebrae

facts.statement: The extreme length of Elasmosaurus's neck was achieved by having a very high number of vertebrae rather than by making individual vertebrae unusually long.
facts.quote: the extreme neck length was achieved by a much increased number of vertebrae

facts.statement: Albertonectes is the only known plesiosaur with more neck vertebrae than Elasmosaurus, possessing at least 75.
facts.quote: Only Albertonectes had more neck vertebrae, at least 75

facts.statement: Having more than 60 neck vertebrae is considered a very derived or advanced trait for plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: more than 60 vertebrae is very derived (or "advanced") for plesiosaurs

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus possessed three pectoral vertebrae, a typical number for the Elasmosauridae family.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus had three pectoral vertebrae, which is a common number for elasmosaurids

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus had four sacral vertebrae, which is the typical number for elasmosaurids.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus had four sacral vertebrae (the fused vertebrae that form the sacrum connected to the pelvis), a number typical of elasmosaurids

facts.statement: The usual number of tail vertebrae for elasmosaurids is 30.
facts.quote: The usual number of tail vertebrae in elasmosaurids is 30

facts.statement: It is possible that the fused tail vertebrae of elasmosaurids supported a tail-fin, though the exact shape of this fin remains unknown.
facts.quote: it is possible this supported a tail-fin, but the shape it would have had is unknown

facts.statement: In 1869, Edward Drinker Cope described the species Elasmosaurus orientalis based on two back vertebrae found in New Jersey.
facts.quote: Accompanying his 1869 description of E. platyurus, Cope named another species of Elasmosaurus, E.orientalis, based on two back vertebrae from New Jersey.

facts.statement: Cope named the species 'orientalis' because he believed it might have a more eastern distribution than E. platyurus.
facts.quote: Cope gave the name orientalis to the new species, on account of it possibly having a more easterly distribution than E.platyurus.

facts.statement: In a 1869 publication, Cope described E. orientalis as having a long neck.
facts.quote: In 1869 Cope also published an article about the fossil reptiles of New Jersey, wherein he described E.orientalis as an animal with a "long neck".

facts.statement: In 1870, Cope admitted that the generic placement of E. orientalis was doubtful and explained that his short-necked illustration was based on his belief that Cimoliasaurus had a short neck.
facts.quote: In an 1870 reply to Leidy, Cope himself stated that the generic placement of E.orientalis was in doubt, and that he had illustrated it with a short neck due to believing this was the condition of Cimoliasaurus.

facts.statement: In 1869, Cope described E. constrictus based on a partial neck vertebra found in Turonian-aged clay deposits at Steyning, Sussex, UK.
facts.quote: In the same 1869 publication wherein he named E. platyurus and E.orientalis, Cope assigned an additional species, E.constrictus, based on a partial centrum from a neck vertebra found in the Turonian-aged clay deposits at Steyning, Sussex, in the United Kingdom.

facts.statement: Richard Owen originally described the specimen as Plesiosaurus constrictus in 1850, naming it for the narrow breadth of the vertebra between the rib-articulating processes.
facts.quote: It was described by the British paleontologist Richard Owen as Plesiosaurus constrictus in 1850; Owen named the species after the extremely narrow breadth of the vertebra between the pleurapophyses, or the processes that articulate between the ribs.

facts.statement: Cope discovered a skeleton in 1876 and named it E. serpentinus in 1877, distinguishing it by features such as un-compressed rear neck vertebrae and few sessile ribs.
facts.quote: Cope discovered another elasmosaurid skeleton in 1876. He named it as a new species, E.serpentinus, in 1877, and differentiated it by the lack of compression in the rear neck vertebrae, the presence of few sessile ribs among the first few dorsals, and the presence of "weak angles" below the front tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: Cope excavated a large skeleton resembling E. orientalis from the 'Cretaceous bed No. 4' black shale with the help of George B. Cledenning and Capt. Nicholas Buesen.
facts.quote: Cope had also discovered another large skeleton that bore great resemblance to the known remains of E.orientalis from the black shale of the "Cretaceous bed No. 4"; he excavated it with the help of George B. Cledenning and Capt. Nicholas Buesen.

facts.statement: John H. Charles found 19 neck and back vertebrae from the Pierre Shale formation in the Big Bend region of Missouri.
facts.quote: Subsequently, a series of 19 neck and back vertebrae from the Big Bend region of the Missouri – part of the Pierre Shale formation – were found by John H. Charles.

facts.statement: Cope named the species E. intermedius in 1894.
facts.quote: He named it E.intermedius in 1894.

facts.statement: In 1906, Williston considered the vertebrae of E. intermedius mutilated and found no distinct differences from E. platyurus.
facts.quote: However, in his 1906 revision of North American plesiosaurs, Williston regarded the vertebrae as "all more or less mutilated", and found no distinct differences between the remains of E.intermedius and E.platyurus.

facts.statement: Welles labeled E. intermedius a nomen dubium in 1962, having previously suggested in 1952 that it should be referred to a pliosaurian genus if valid.
facts.quote: In 1952 Welles opined that, if E.intermedius was valid, "it must be referred to a pliosaurian genus"; however, he proceeded to label it a nomen dubium in 1962.

facts.statement: Most species of Elasmosaurus described after the type species E. platyurus are now considered dubious names or have been moved to other genera.
facts.quote: Following the description of the type species, E. platyurus, a number of other Elasmosaurus species were described by Cope, Williston, and other authors. However, none of these species are still definitely referable to the genus Elasmosaurus today, and most of them either have been moved to genera of their own or are considered dubious names, nomina dubia – that is, with no distinguishing features, and therefore of questionable validity.

facts.statement: Leidy transferred E. orientalis to the genus Discosaurus the year after Cope's description.
facts.quote: Leidy subsequently moved E.orientalis to the now dubious genus Discosaurus in the following year.

facts.statement: Welles considered E. orientalis a nomen dubium in 1952 due to its fragmentary nature.
facts.quote: In 1952 Welles considered the species a nomen dubium, given how fragmentary it was.

facts.statement: Welles moved E. serpentinus to the new genus Hydralmosaurus in 1943.
facts.quote: In 1943 Welles removed E.serpentinus from Elasmosaurus, and placed it in a new genus, Hydralmosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2016, all specimens previously assigned to Hydralmosaurus were moved to Styxosaurus, making Hydralmosaurus a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: Subsequently, all Hydralmosaurus specimens were moved to Styxosaurus in 2016, rendering the former a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: Welles assigned a specimen of E. serpentinus to the new species Alzadasaurus riggsi in 1943.
facts.quote: Welles moved this specimen to the new genus and species Alzadasaurus riggsi in 1943.

facts.statement: Carpenter reassigned a specimen to Thalassomedon haningtoni in 1999, but later researchers noted it was a distorted juvenile and preferred to keep it as a nomen dubium in 2016.
facts.quote: Kenneth Carpenter reassigned it to Thalassomedon haningtoni in 1999; Sachs, Johan Lindgren, and Benjamin Kear noted that the remains represented a juvenile and were significantly distorted, and preferred to retain it as a nomen dubium in 2016.

facts.statement: Welles considered the genus Embaphias and its species E. circulosus a nomen dubium in 1962.
facts.quote: Three shorter vertebrae found alongside E.intermedius, assigned by Cope to the new genus and species Embaphias circulosus, were also considered by Welles to be a nomen dubium in 1962.

facts.statement: A specimen of Elasmosaurus was discovered in Plum Creek, Kansas, in 1874 by Williston and Mudge.
facts.quote: In 1874 he and Mudge discovered a specimen in Plum Creek, Kansas.

facts.statement: Elias West discovered a second Elasmosaurus specimen in 1890.
facts.quote: A second specimen, discovered by Elias West in 1890, was also assigned by him to E.snowii.

facts.statement: Handel Martin found an elasmosaurid specimen in Logan County, Kansas, in 1889.
facts.quote: An elasmosaurid specimen was found by Handel Martin in Logan County, Kansas in 1889.

facts.statement: Very large remains of Elasmosaurus were discovered by Mudge in Jewell County, Kansas, in 1874.
facts.quote: Another species, E.nobilis, was named by Williston from very large remains discovered by Mudge in 1874 in Jewell County, Kansas.

facts.statement: Charles Sternberg collected two exceptionally large dorsal vertebrae in 1895 which were named Elasmosaurus sternbergii.
facts.quote: Finally, two exceptionally large dorsal vertebrae collected by Charles Sternberg in 1895 were named E.sternbergii by Williston

facts.statement: Anatoly Riabinin described a single flipper phalanx as Elasmosaurus sachalinensis in 1915.
facts.quote: Anatoly Riabinin described a single phalanx from a flipper in 1915 as E.(?)sachalinensis

facts.statement: Pavel A. Pravoslavlev named Elasmosaurus amalitskii in 1916 based on a specimen from the Don River region containing vertebrae, limb girdles, and limb bones.
facts.quote: Then, in 1916, Pavel A. Pravoslavlev named E.amalitskii from the Don River region, based on a specimen containing vertebrae, limb girdles, and limb bones.

facts.statement: Welles named the species Elasmosaurus morgani in 1949 from a well-preserved skeleton found in Dallas County, Texas.
facts.quote: In 1949 Welles named a new species of Elasmosaurus, E.morgani. It was named from a well-preserved skeleton found in Dallas County, Texas.

facts.statement: Dubeikovskii and Ochev named Elasmosaurus antiquus in 1967 from fossils found in the Kamsko-Vyatsky phosphorite quarry.
facts.quote: Another species from Russia, E.antiquus, was named by Dubeikovskii and Ochev in 1967 from the Kamsko-Vyatsky phosphorite quarry

facts.statement: The validity of several Russian species previously assigned to Elasmosaurus has been questioned by researchers.
facts.quote: However, the validity of all these species has been questioned.

facts.statement: Researchers have debated whether the Swedish species Elasmosaurus helmerseni is closely related to Elasmosaurus proper, noting the material was too fragmentary to confirm this in 1959.
facts.quote: Persson noted in a 1959 review of the Swedish "E."helmerseni material that, while the species was probably closely related to Elasmosaurus proper, it was too fragmentary for this hypothesis to be assessed

facts.statement: As of 2017, the New Zealand species Mauisaurus haasti (formerly assigned to Elasmosaurus) is regarded as a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: Although its validity was supported for a considerable time, M.haasti is regarded as a nomen dubium as of 2017.

facts.statement: Welles recognized the New Zealand species Elasmosaurus hoodii as a nomen dubium in 1962.
facts.quote: Welles recognized it as a nomen dubium in 1962

facts.statement: As of 2013, the attribution of the species Elasmosaurus gigas to the genus Elasmosaurus remains questionable.
facts.quote: As of 2013, this questionable attribution remains unchanged.

facts.statement: Welles moved the species Elasmosaurus snowii to the genus Styxosaurus in 1943.
facts.quote: In 1943 Welles moved E.snowii to its own genus, Styxosaurus, where the species has remained.

facts.statement: Welles assigned two Elasmosaurus specimens to the new genus Thalassiosaurus in 1943.
facts.quote: In 1943 both specimens were assigned to the new genus Thalassiosaurus by Welles

facts.statement: Glenn Storrs considered two Elasmosaurus specimens to be indeterminate elasmosaurids in 1999.
facts.quote: Glenn Storrs considered both to be indeterminate elasmosaurids in 1999

facts.statement: Carpenter placed Elasmosaurus morgani in its own genus, Libonectes, in 1997.
facts.quote: In 1997 Carpenter reconsidered the differences between the two species, and found them sufficient to place E.morgani in its own genus, which he named Libonectes.

facts.statement: Persson assigned the species Elasmosaurus gigas to the genus Elasmosaurus in 1959.
facts.quote: Persson assigned another species to Elasmosaurus alongside his 1959 description of "E."helmerseni remains from Sweden, namely E.(?)gigas.

facts.statement: Pervushov and colleagues reinterpreted Elasmosaurus antiquus as an indeterminate elasmosaurid in 1999.
facts.quote: Pervushov and colleagues in 1999, followed by Storrs and colleagues in 2000, reinterpreted it as an indeterminate elasmosaurid.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope originally classified Elasmosaurus as a plesiosaur but placed it in a new order called Streptosauria in a 1869 paper.
facts.quote: Though Cope had originally recognized Elasmosaurus as a plesiosaur, in an 1869 paper he placed it, with Cimoliasaurus and Crymocetus, in a new order of sauropterygian reptiles.

facts.statement: Cope distinguished Elasmosaurus from Cimoliasaurus by its longer neck with compressed vertebrae versus a shorter neck with square, depressed vertebrae.
facts.quote: Within this family, he considered the former to be distinguished by a longer neck with compressed vertebrae, and the latter by a shorter neck with square, depressed vertebrae.

facts.statement: Welles united Elasmosaurus and Brancasaurus in the subfamily Elasmosaurinae in 1962 based on their sharing of completely closed pelvic bars formed from fused ischia.
facts.quote: In 1962 Welles further subdivided elasmosaurids based on whether they possessed pelvic bars formed from the fusion of the ischia, with Elasmosaurus and Brancasaurus being united in the subfamily Elasmosaurinae by their sharing of completely closed pelvic bars.

facts.statement: Sachs suggested Elasmosaurus was closely related to Styxosaurus in 2005, while Druckenmiller and Russell placed it in a polytomy with Libonectes, Terminonatator, Callawayasaurus, and Hydrotherosaurus in 2008.
facts.quote: In 2005 Sachs suggested that Elasmosaurus was closely related to Styxosaurus, and in 2008 Druckenmiller and Russell placed it as part of a polytomy with two groups, one containing Libonectes and Terminonatator, the other containing Callawayasaurus and Hydrotherosaurus.

facts.statement: Otero's 2016 analysis placed Elasmosaurus as the closest relative of Albertonectes, forming the Styxosaurinae with Styxosaurus and Terminonatator.
facts.quote: In Rodrigo Otero's 2016 analysis based on a modification of the same dataset (below, right), Elamosaurus was the closest relative of Albertonectes, forming the Styxosaurinae with Styxosaurus and Terminonatator.

facts.statement: O'Gorman formally synonymized Styxosaurinae with Elasmosaurinae in 2020 based on the inclusion of Elasmosaurus within the group.
facts.quote: In 2020, O'Gorman formally synonymized Styxosaurinae with Elasmosaurinae based on the inclusion of Elasmosaurus within the group, and also provided a list of diagnostic characteristics for the clade.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurids were fully adapted to ocean life with streamlined bodies and long paddles indicating they were active swimmers.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurids were fully adapted to life in the ocean, with streamlined bodies and long paddles that indicate they were active swimmers.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence shows elasmosaurids were preyed upon, including a humerus with bite marks from the shark Cretoxyrhina and a crushed Eromangasaurus skull with tooth marks from the pliosaur Kronosaurus.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurid remains provide some evidence they were preyed upon. A humerus of an unidentified subadult elasmosaurid was found with bite marks matching the teeth of the shark Cretoxyrhina, while a crushed Eromangasaurus skull has tooth-marks matched to the pliosaur Kronosaurus.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope compared the build and habits of Elasmosaurus to those of a snake in 1869.
facts.quote: Cope, in 1869, compared the build and habits of Elasmosaurus with those of a snake.

facts.statement: Cope envisioned the snake-like head of Elasmosaurus being raised high, arched like a swan before striking fish, or stretched while resting on the water.
facts.quote: The snake-like head was raised high in the air, or depressed at the will of the animal, now arched swan-like preparatory to a plunge after a fish, now stretched in repose on the water or deflexed in exploring the depths below

facts.statement: A study found elasmosaurid necks could move 75–177 degrees ventrally, 87–155 degrees dorsally, and 94–176 degrees laterally.
facts.quote: One study found that the necks of elasmosaurids were capable of 75–177˚ of ventral movement, 87–155° of dorsal movement, and 94–176° of lateral movement

facts.statement: It is debated whether the long necks of plesiosaurs acted as snorkels, as this theory faces disputes regarding large hydrostatic pressure differences.
facts.quote: It has also been suggested that the long necks of plesiosaurs served as a snorkel and allowed them to breathe air while the body remained underwater. This is disputed as there would be large hydrostatic pressure differences

facts.statement: In 1869, Cope found scales and teeth from six fish species beneath the vertebrae of the Elasmosaurus holotype.
facts.quote: In 1869 Cope noted that scales and teeth of six species of fish had been discovered directly beneath the vertebrae of the Elasmosaurus holotype

facts.statement: Elasmosaurids may have hunted in the pelagic zone by retracting their necks to strike or using side-swipe motions to stun prey with their teeth.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurids may also have been active hunters in the pelagic zone, retracting their necks to launch a strike or using side-swipe motions to stun or kill prey with their laterally projected teeth

facts.statement: Elasmosaurids likely ate small bony fish and cephalopods because their skulls limited the size of prey they could consume.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurids probably ate small bony fish and Cephalopods, as their small, non-kinetic skulls would have limited the size of the prey they could eat.

facts.statement: At its largest, the Western Interior Seaway stretched from the Rockies to the Appalachians, approximately 1000 km wide.
facts.quote: At its largest, the Western Interior Seaway stretched from the Rockies east to the Appalachians, some 1000 km wide.

facts.statement: The genus Elasmosaurus was established by Cope in 1868.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Cope, 1868

facts.statement: The species E. platyurus is a subdivision of the genus Elasmosaurus.
facts.quote: subdivision: E. platyurus

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus is a genus of elasmosaurid plesiosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now the United States.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus (del griego ελασμος elasmos 'placa delgada', refiriéndose a las placas delgadas de su pelvis + σαυρος sauros 'lagarto') es un género representado por una especie de plesiosauroide elasmosáurido que vivió en el Cretácico Superior, en lo que hoy es Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus was a marine reptile with an extremely long neck that lived during the Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 80.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus fue un reptil marino con un cuello extremadamente largo que vivió en el período Cretácico Superior (edad del Campaniense), hace 80,5 millones de años.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus measured about 14 meters in length and weighed about 2000 kilograms, making it one of the largest plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus medía cerca de 14 metros de largo y pesaba cerca de 2000 kilogramos, lo que lo convierte en uno de los mayores plesiosaurios.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus differs from other plesiosaurs by having six teeth per premaxilla and 71 cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: Difiere de otros plesiosaurios por tener seis dientes por premaxilar (los huesos en la punta del hocico) y 71 vértebras cervicales.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus is the only known plesiosaur with more than 70 cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus es el único plesiosaurio conocido con más de 70 cervicales.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus had more vertebrae than any other known animal.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus tenía más vértebras que cualquier otro animal conocido.

facts.statement: The skull of Elasmosaurus was relatively thin and flattened, barely more voluminous than the neck itself.
facts.quote: El cráneo era relativamente delgado y aplanado, apenas más voluminoso que el propio cuello.

facts.statement: Its pointed snout provided an aerodynamic silhouette allowing faster movement through water, and its sharp teeth were used to catch mollusks rather than crush their shells.
facts.quote: El apuntado hocico le proporcionaba una silueta aerodinámica, que le permitía desplazarse a mayor velocidad a través del agua, con varios dientes aguzados, que no podían aplastar conchas de los moluscos, pero si atraparlos en la boca para luego engullirlos.

facts.statement: The cervical vertebrae immediately following the skull were long, low, and had longitudinal lateral crests.
facts.quote: Las vértebras del cuello que siguen inmediatamente al cráneo eran largas y bajas y tenían crestas longitudinales laterales.

facts.statement: Like many elasmosaurids, Elasmosaurus had about three pectoral vertebrae.
facts.quote: Como muchos elasmosáuridos, Elasmosaurus tenía cerca de tres vértebras pectorales.

facts.statement: The tail of Elasmosaurus included at least 18 vertebrae.
facts.quote: La cola incluía al menos 18 vértebras.

facts.statement: The shoulder girdle of Elasmosaurus featured a long bony bar that was not present in juveniles.
facts.quote: La cintura escapular presentaba una larga vara ósea, no presente en los juveniles.

facts.statement: The limbs of Elasmosaurus were modified into four approximately equal-sized oar-shaped flippers, like other plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: Los miembros de Elasmosaurus, como los de otros plesiosaurios, estaban modificados en cuatro aletas en forma de remo de un tamaño aproximadamente igual.

facts.statement: The presence of the pectoral bar is considered an advanced characteristic in Elasmosaurus.
facts.quote: La presencia de la vara pectoral es también considerada una característica avanzada.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus platyurus was described in March 1868 by Edward Drinker Cope based on a fossil discovered and collected by Dr. Theophilus Turner in western Kansas, United States.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus platyurus fue descrito en marzo de 1868 por Edward Drinker Cope a partir de un fósil descubierto y recolectado por el Dr. Theophilus Turner, un médico militar, al oeste de Kansas, Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: When E. D. Cope received the specimen in early March 1868, he incorrectly placed the head at the wrong end, at the tail, due to preconceived ideas about lizard anatomy.
facts.quote: Cuando E. D. Cope recibió el espécimen a principios de marzo de 1868, él tenía una idea preconcebida de como debía de lucir, y erradamente situó la cabeza en el extremo equivocado (es decir, al final de la cola).

facts.statement: Joseph Leidy actually pointed out the error in his speech 'Considerations on Elasmosaurus platyurus' at the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia on March 8, 1870.
facts.quote: fue realmente Joseph Leidy quien señaló el problema en su discurso Consideraciones sobre Elasmosaurus platyurus en un encuentro de la Academia de Ciencias Naturales de Philadelphia el 8 de marzo de 1870.

facts.statement: Although numerous species of Elasmosaurus have been named, a 1999 review by Ken Carpenter showed that only the type species Elasmosaurus platyurus could be considered valid.
facts.quote: Aunque numerosas especies de Elasmosaurus han sido nombradas desde su descubrimiento, una revisión de 1999 hecha por Ken Carpenter mostró que sólo una de estas, la especie tipo Elasmosaurus platyurus, podría ser considerada válida.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus is the type genus for the elasmosaurids, a group characterized by extremely long necks and small heads, contrasting with polycotylids which had short necks and relatively large heads.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus es el género tipo para uno de estos grupos, los elasmosáuridos que tenían cuellos extremadamente alargados con cabezas pequeñas, en contraste con los policotílidos que tenían cuellos cortos y cabezas relativamente grandes.

facts.statement: It has been suggested that Elasmosaurus was closely related to Hydralmosaurus and Styxosaurus due to these advanced traits.
facts.quote: Se ha sugerido que Elasmosaurus estaba cercanamente relacionado con Hydralmosaurus y a Styxosaurus debido a estos rasgos avanzados.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous (Campanian age), approximately 80.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus fue un reptil marino con un cuello extremadamente largo que vivió en el período Cretácico Superior (edad del Campaniense), hace 80,5 millones de años.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus had approximately three pectoral vertebrae, a trait shared with many other elasmosaurids.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus tenía cerca de tres vértebras pectorales.

facts.statement: The long and low axis of the vertebral centrum in Elasmosaurus differs from many other plesiosaurs, which have centers shorter in length than in height, or nearly equal in dimensions.
facts.quote: El largo y bajo eje del centro de la vértebra difiere de la condición vista en muchos otros plesiosaurios, que tienen centros más cortos en longitud que en altura, o casi iguales en dimensisones.

facts.statement: While long-necked Jurassic plesiosaurs from England were already well known, Elasmosaurus was the first known from the Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Aunque eran mucho menores, por entonces ya eran bien conocidos los plesiosaurios de cuello largo del Jurásico de Inglaterra, pero Elasmosaurus era el primero que se conocía del Cretácico.

facts.statement: Fossils of Elasmosaurus have been found in Campanian-age Upper Cretaceous strata of the Pierre Shale formation in western Kansas.
facts.quote: Los fósiles de Elasmosaurus se han hallado en los estratos de edad del Campaniense del Cretácico Superior de la formación Pierre Shale del oeste de Kansas.

facts.statement: The formation represents a marine deposition period of the Niobrara Sea, a shallow inland sea located over central North America during the Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Esta formación representa un período de deposición marina del Mar de Niobrara, un mar continental poco profundo que se encontraba sobre la parte central de Norteamérica durante el Cretácico.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus was a slow swimmer that likely ambushed schools of fish.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus era un lento nadador y pudo haber acechado a los cardúmenes de peces.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus likely ate small bony fish, belemnites (similar to squids), and ammonites (mollusks).
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus probablemente comía pequeños peces óseos, belemnites (similares a los calamares), y ammonites (moluscos).

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus also swallowed small stones to aid its digestion.
facts.quote: También engullía pequeñas piedras para ayudar a su digestión.

facts.statement: It is believed that Elasmosaurus lived mostly in open oceans.
facts.quote: Se cree que Elasmosaurus viviría mayormente en océanos abiertos.

facts.statement: The flippers of Elasmosaurus and other plesiosaurs were very rigid and specialized for swimming, preventing them from reaching land to lay eggs.
facts.quote: La aletas de Elasmosaurus y otros plesiosaurios eran muy rígidas y especializadas para nadar y no pudieron haberles permitido llegar a tierra para depositar sus huevos.

facts.statement: Therefore, it is most likely that they gave birth to live young like modern sea snakes.
facts.quote: Por lo tanto lo más probable es que dieran a luz crías vivas como las actuales serpientes marinas.

facts.statement: The genus Elasmosaurus was named by Cope in 1868.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Elasmosaurus (genus), Cope 1868

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus belongs to the parent group Elasmosaurinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Elasmosaurinae

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus is classified in the family Elasmosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Elasmosauridae

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus is classified in the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus lived from the Turonian to the Campanian stages, between 93.9 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Turonian to Campanian (93.9 to 72.2 million years ago)
